The Slonimer Rebbe's supper
The Rav says that when a person needs a yeshuah he should mention the names of tzaddikim, which brings kedushah upon him.
The Rav says a person should guard and strengthen his name and sanctify it, so that mentioning it will bring down blessing.
The Rav says that at hagbah everyone should look at the letters of the Sefer Torah and become holier from it.

Why mention the names of the Chachamim
The power of speech
Rav Shimon Sofer and the holy name
Chevron on Yom Kippur; a name is the neshamah
Adam's names and Rabbi Meir's neshamah
Torah lishmah merits many things
The holier, the easier to spoil
Words of Torah said with ruach hakodesh contain much in few words, so several explanations of the same Chazal can all be true.
Mentioning the name of a Chacham is not an interruption in learning, because the name itself has become Torah.
Every word a Jew speaks has an effect in the world and above it: a good word builds and brings blessing, a bad word destroys.
A Jewish name is made of holy letters that are the substance of the neshamah, so mentioning a Tanna's name activates his neshamah and connects the learner to him.
The Tanna does not spell out the 'many things' that one who learns Torah lishmah merits, because his Olam Haba is too holy for even the Nevi'im to see.
The Rav reads 'baruch shebachar bahem uvemishnasam' not only as praise of Hashem but as praise of the talmid who chose to devote his life to these Chachamim and their Torah.
The halachic fact that saying a Chacham's name is not a hefsek in learning Torah shows that his name itself has become Torah.
The oversized fruit of Eretz Yisrael in the meraglim's time came from the abnormal amount of Torah being learned in the Midbar, since every good word builds and blesses the world.

Unlike an English word such as 'lion', which is only an agreed label, the Hebrew name aryeh is made of the very letters that give the lion its existence and character; a Tanna's name likewise is the substance of his neshamah.
Saying 'Rabbi Meir' before his halacha is more than honor: it draws part of his neshamah into the learner, just as Moshe Rabbeinu was endowed with the power of a holy name when he said it.
The more holy something is, the more easily it is spoiled, as with levels of tumah and with wine; this is why the Olam Haba of one who learns Torah lishmah may not be seen at all.
Why does the Gemara spend so much time repeating the names of the Chachamim, even where it makes no practical difference who said it?
How could David HaMelech have had in mind everything later written on Tehillim?
Why did the announcement on Yom Kippur morning mention Chevron, which is far from Yerushalayim?
Why does the Tanna not say what the 'many things' are that one who learns Torah lishmah merits?

The Rav says that saying a Tanna's name before his halacha makes contact with his neshamah, and that this makes the halacha easier to understand.
